questions.question_text: Under the Statute of Frauds, South Dakota real estate contracts must be:
questions.correct_answer: In writing and signed by the parties
distractors: Notarized and recorded at the county office
Witnessed by two disinterested parties
Approved by the SDREC before execution
questions.explanation: Real estate contracts must be in writing and signed to satisfy the statute of frauds. Brokerage-service agreements must also be on forms substantially the same as those the commission prescribes (ARSD 20:69:17:01), and every signer gets a copy.

questions.question_text: A buyer signs a counteroffer but the seller does not. Is this a binding contract in South Dakota?
questions.correct_answer: No, both parties must sign for enforceability
distractors: Yes, the buyer's signature alone creates a contract
Yes, if the counteroffer was delivered in writing
No, but the buyer is still bound by their signature
questions.explanation: A counteroffer binds no one until both parties sign it. The licensee must promptly give a copy of the offer to the buyer, every written offer to the seller, and a copy of the signed acceptance to both (SDCL 36-21A-71(19)–(21)).

questions.question_text: Which element is NOT typically required in a South Dakota purchase agreement?
questions.correct_answer: The buyer's credit score and employment history
distractors: The purchase price and legal description
The closing date and earnest money terms
The financing type and possession date
questions.explanation: A purchase agreement prepared by a licensee must show the parties, price, earnest money receipt, disclosure acknowledgments, financing and inspection contingencies, prorations, merchantable title, closing, and possession (ARSD 20:69:17:01). The buyer's credit score is a lending matter.

questions.question_text: A seller tells a licensee to keep everything the property sells for above $300,000 as the fee. May the licensee take the listing on those terms?
questions.correct_answer: No, that is a prohibited net listing
distractors: Yes, if the seller agrees in writing
Yes, if the excess is capped at 10 percent
Yes, if the listing is non-exclusive
questions.explanation: Taking a net listing — agreeing to be paid the sale proceeds above a price set in the listing contract — is unprofessional conduct in South Dakota (SDCL 36-21A-71(26)). The seller's written consent does not cure it.

questions.question_text: In a South Dakota contract for deed, who retains legal ownership until the contract is fully paid?
distractors: The buyer
The title company
The responsible broker
questions.explanation: In a contract for deed, the seller remains the legal owner until the contract is fully paid. The buyer makes monthly payments directly to the seller. This arrangement is used when traditional mortgage financing cannot be obtained.

questions.question_text: A buyer offers a promissory note instead of cash as earnest money. May the licensee accept it?
questions.correct_answer: Only with the principal's written permission
distractors: Yes, a note is always acceptable earnest money
No, South Dakota requires cash or a certified check
Yes, if the note is payable before closing
questions.explanation: Accepting a note or anything else not readily negotiable as earnest money without the written permission of the licensee's principal is unprofessional conduct (SDCL 36-21A-71(38)). With that written permission the note is allowed.

questions.question_text: An earnest money dispute involves $10,000. Can this be resolved in Small Claims Court?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, disputes of $12,000 or less qualify
distractors: No, earnest money disputes cannot go to small claims
No, the threshold is only $5,000
Yes, but only if both parties consent
questions.explanation: Small claims jurisdiction runs to $12,000, which covers most earnest money fights (SDCL 15-39-45). The commission does not decide who gets the deposit; disputed funds stay in trust until all parties agree in writing or a court rules.

questions.question_text: A buyer's financing contingency expires and financing was not obtained. What happens to the contract?
questions.correct_answer: The contract ends with no legal obligation
distractors: The buyer must find alternative financing
The seller can force the sale to proceed
The earnest money is automatically forfeited
questions.explanation: If a contingency cannot be met within its specified timeframe, the contract ends with no legal obligation to either party. Common contingencies include financing, inspection, appraisal, and sale of existing property.

questions.question_text: A seller adds a clause requiring the buyer to remove their sale contingency within 48 hours or the seller can accept another offer. This is called a:
distractors: Acceleration clause
Due-on-sale clause
Liquidated damages clause
questions.explanation: A seller may add a time clause (also called a kick-out or bump clause) requiring the buyer to remove contingencies within a specified period. This protects the seller from being locked into a contract while the buyer's existing property remains unsold.

questions.question_text: In a cobrokerage transaction, where must the earnest money be held?
distractors: With the title company handling closing
Split between the two cooperating brokers
In the listing broker's operating account
questions.explanation: Earnest money paid in a cooperative or cobrokerage transaction is held in a broker's trust account unless the buyer and seller agree otherwise (SDCL 36-21A-76). How the brokers split the fee has no bearing on where the money sits.
